explanation: SET NOCOUNT OFF explicitly leaves row-count DONE messages enabled for every statement, adding client and network chatter; the procedure should set SET NOCOUNT ON.
SET XACT_ABORT OFF is explicitly disabled although this procedure uses BEGIN TRANSACTION, so some run-time errors can leave a transaction partially applied.
SELECT * on Sales.Orders returns all 16 columns and couples callers to every current and future column of the table.
TOP (10) without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary, non-deterministic set of rows from Sales.Orders.
DISTINCT on o.OrderID is redundant because OrderID is the primary key of Sales.Orders and is already unique.
WITH (NOLOCK) on Sales.Orders can return uncommitted, missing, or duplicated rows.
YEAR(o.OrderDate) applies a function to the filtered date column, preventing an index seek; use a range predicate on OrderDate instead.
o.CustomerID (int) is compared with @CustomerIdText (nvarchar), forcing an implicit conversion of the column side and degrading cardinality estimates and sargability.
(@CustomerID IS NULL OR o.CustomerID = @CustomerID) is an OR-based optional filter that defeats consistent index seeks and produces unstable plans.
LIKE N'%urgent%' starts with a wildcard, preventing a normal index seek on Comments.
NOT IN (SELECT i.CustomerID FROM Sales.Invoices) returns no rows at all if the subquery ever yields NULL; use NOT EXISTS instead.
ISNULL(o.CustomerID, 0) = 1 wraps the CustomerID column in a function, making the predicate non-sargable.
o.OrderID + 0 = @OrderID applies arithmetic to the indexed OrderID column, preventing a direct index seek.
o.CustomerID <> 1 is an inequality predicate that typically forces scans of broad index ranges.
CROSS JOIN between Sales.Orders and Sales.Customers has no join predicate and multiplies every order by every customer.
TOP (1) without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary row of the cross product.
Sales.Orders and Sales.OrderLines are comma-separated in FROM with the join condition in WHERE; use ANSI JOIN syntax.
TOP (1) without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary row.
The correlated scalar subquery (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE ol.OrderID = o.OrderID) executes once per outer order row; rewrite as a JOIN with GROUP BY.
The correlated EXISTS against Sales.OrderLines runs per outer row instead of being expressed as a set-based semi join.
CASE WHEN o.Comments IS NULL THEN 0 ELSE 1 END is duplicated in the SELECT list and the ORDER BY; compute it once via a derived table or CROSS APPLY.
ORDER BY 2 references the select list by position, which silently breaks if the column order changes.
OFFSET/FETCH pages ordered only by o.OrderDate, which is not unique, so rows can shift between pages; add a unique tie-breaker such as o.OrderID.
The two branches filter OrderID = 1 and OrderID = 2 and are disjoint by construction, so UNION's duplicate elimination is needless work.
(SELECT COUNT(*) FROM Sales.OrderLines ...) > 0 counts all matching rows when only existence matters; use EXISTS.
SELECT @OrderID = o.OrderID silently keeps the last row's value if multiple rows match; use SET with TOP (1) and ORDER BY instead.
Table variable @OrderIds receives a fixed low-row cardinality estimate, which skews plans for non-trivial row counts; prefer a temp table.
INSERT ... SELECT TOP (5) without ORDER BY loads an arbitrary set of orders into @OrderIds.
SELECT ... INTO #ImplicitOrders creates the temp table schema implicitly; declare the table explicitly with CREATE TABLE.
TOP (5) without ORDER BY selects an arbitrary set of rows into #ImplicitOrders.
A cursor with OPEN/FETCH NEXT processes orders row by row; this work can be expressed set-wise.
The cursor's SELECT TOP (2) has no ORDER BY, so the fetched rows are arbitrary.
WHILE @Counter <= 1 performs iterative row-by-row style work instead of a set-based operation.
The dynamic SQL string is built by concatenating CONVERT(nvarchar(20), @CustomerID) into the statement text; use sys.sp_executesql with a bound parameter.
EXEC (@Sql) executes the concatenated string with no parameterization; use sys.sp_executesql with typed parameters.
The dynamic SQL string embeds the OrderID value by concatenation instead of binding it as a parameter.
sys.sp_executesql is invoked without any parameter definitions even though a value is embedded in the string.
#Scratch is created with CREATE TABLE and never dropped before the procedure ends.
The CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() as IgnoredError; it neither rethrows with THROW nor returns a failure status, hiding the error.
RAISERROR is used for a new error path; THROW preserves the original error number and state and is the modern alternative.
PRINT output is buffered and client-dependent, making it unsuitable for structured diagnostics.
o.CustomerID = 1 embeds a business identifier directly in the query instead of accepting it as a parameter or looking it up.
'20160101' is an unlabelled date constant embedded in the filter logic; use a typed date parameter or variable.
CONVERT(date, '01/02/2016') omits the style parameter, so the parsed value depends on session language and DATEFORMAT settings.
COALESCE(o.CustomerID, 0) = COALESCE(i.CustomerID, 0) wraps both join columns in functions, inhibiting index seeks and efficient join strategies.
TOP (1) without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary row.
Sales.Orders is self-joined on o.OrderID = o2.OrderID, retrieving only information already available in the same row.
TOP (1) without ORDER BY returns an arbitrary row.
ORDER BY o.Comments sorts on an nvarchar(MAX) LOB column, forcing an expensive, unselective sort.
SUM(ol.Quantity) aggregates the entire fact-like Sales.OrderLines table with no restrictive filter.
HAVING ol.OrderID > 0 applies a row-level predicate after grouping; move it to WHERE to filter rows before aggregation.
The aggregate without GROUP BY returns a single row, so ORDER BY OrderCount is meaningless.
MERGE has documented concurrency and correctness edge cases; use separate UPDATE and INSERT statements.
SET Comments = Comments writes the existing value back, causing logging and locking without changing any data.
DELETE FROM Sales.OrderLines WHERE Quantity = -1 uses a broad, non-key predicate that can remove many unrelated rows.
WAITFOR DELAY '00:00:01' intentionally blocks a worker thread; use asynchronous scheduling instead.
BEGIN TRANSACTION is not wrapped in TRY/CATCH, so an error before ROLLBACK can leave an orphaned open transaction.
SET IDENTITY_INSERT Sales.Orders ON changes session identity handling and is fragile if the table schema changes.
EXEC sp_who calls the system procedure without a schema qualifier, forcing a master-database name resolution lookup first.
SET ROWCOUNT 1 is never reset to 0, silently limiting the rows returned by all subsequent statements in the session.
INSERT INTO #DemoCategories VALUES (...) omits an explicit column list and will break if the table's column order changes.
LIKE '%' + @CustomerName + '%' starts with a wildcard, preventing index seeks on Sales.Customers.CustomerName.
The dynamic SQL string is built by concatenating @CustomerName directly into the LIKE pattern text.
User-supplied @CustomerName is concatenated directly into the executed SQL string, enabling SQL injection; use a parameterized sys.sp_executesql call.
sp_executesql runs the concatenated string without any declared parameters.
sp_executesql is invoked without the sys. schema qualifier.
UPDATE #DemoCustomers SET CustomerCategoryID = 1 has no WHERE clause and overwrites the category of every row in the table.
The WHERE predicate on the left-joined Sales.Orders (o.OrderDate >= ...) turns the LEFT JOIN into an inner join, silently dropping customers without orders.
'2016-01-01' is an unlabelled date constant embedded in the query logic.
WHERE DeliveryMethodID = NULL never evaluates to true because NULL comparisons yield UNKNOWN; use IS NULL instead.
dbo.GetCustomerType(CustomerID) is a scalar UDF evaluated row by row for every customer, preventing parallel, set-based execution.
The CATCH block handles an error raised after BEGIN TRANSACTION without rolling back, leaving an open transaction holding locks.
The CATCH block only selects ERROR_MESSAGE() and neither rethrows with THROW nor signals failure.
WITH (INDEX = 1) hardcodes an index choice on Sales.Customers, which breaks if indexes change and overrides the optimizer.
Three levels of nested derived tables (t1, t2, t3) each projecting only CustomerID add no value; refactor into a single query or a CTE.
LIKE '%A%' starts with a wildcard, preventing an index seek on Sales.Customers.CustomerName.
SELECT * from dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti returns all columns, coupling callers to the function's output schema.
dbo.GetCustomerOrdersMulti is a multi-statement table-valued function, which materializes results into a work table with fixed cardinality estimates; an inline TVF would optimize better.
